title: 論語 述而第七
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 7, 〈述而〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 7 of the Analects, 述而 Shù ér, named, as every book is, from its first words ("transmitting, and…"). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi says this book mostly records the Master's words about himself, always modest ones, and his teaching, together with what he was like and what he did. It opens with him calling himself a transmitter, not a maker (7.1), and dreaming no longer of the Duke of Zhou (7.5); it shows him at ease at home (7.4), refusing to eat his fill beside the bereaved (7.9), so carried away by the Shao music in Qi that for three months he did not notice the taste of meat (7.13), content with coarse rice, water and a bent arm for a pillow (7.15), and sure that Heaven's gift in him was beyond the reach of a man who wanted him dead (7.22). Some of the most quoted lines of the whole Analects are here: the Master not speaking of prodigies, feats of strength, disorder or spirits (7.20), finding a teacher in any two companions on the road (7.21), humaneness arriving the moment one wants it (7.29), and the gentleman calm and broad where the small man is forever anxious (7.36). The book closes on a picture of him: warm yet stern, commanding without harshness, respectful and at ease (7.37). Each numbered passage (7.1–7.37, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 7.28 the edition we follow misprints 已 for 己 'oneself'; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
述而不作，
信而好古，
竊比於我老彭。」

morph.gloss: Old Peng — a worthy grandee of Shang

sentences.i: The Master said: “I hand down what I received and invent nothing; I trust the ways of old and love them. If I may, I would set myself beside our Old Peng.”
sentences.n: The book is named 述而 from its first words. Zhu Xi heads it: it mostly records the sage's words of self-effacement and of teaching others, and the facts of his bearing and conduct — thirty-seven chapters in all. 述 shù is 'to hand on what is old', 作 'to start something new' (Zhu Xi: 述，傳舊而已；作，則創始也); only a sage can originate, a worthy can transmit. 而 joins the paired verbs: 'but' in the first line, 'and' in the second. 好 is hào 'to love' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 竊 qiè is literally 'to steal': before a verb of one's own it means 'privately, presuming' — Zhu Xi calls 竊比 a word of deference toward Old Peng, and 我 'our' a word of intimacy. 老彭 Old Peng, Zhu Xi says, was a worthy grandee of Shang, who appears in the Da Dai Liji, probably one who trusted antiquity and transmitted it; He Yan's Bao Xian: a worthy grandee of Yin (= Shang), fond of transmitting ancient things — 'I am like Old Peng, I only transmit.' Zhu Xi: Confucius edited the Odes and the Documents, settled the rites and music, wrote in praise of the Changes and compiled the Spring and Autumn — all handing on what the former kings left, never originating; so he did not dare claim a creator's sagehood, nor even openly attach himself to the worthies of old, his heart growing lower as his virtue grew fuller. Yet by then the work of creation was nearly complete, and the Master gathered the great achievement of all the sages and weighed it: the task was transmission, but its merit was double that of creating.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
黙而識之，
學而不厭，
誨人不倦，
何有於我哉？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Silently to keep it in mind,
to learn and never have one's fill,
to teach others and never weary of it —
which of these is there in me?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “To take things in without a word and hold on to them, to study and never feel I have studied enough, to teach others and never weary of it — which of these can I claim?”
sentences.n: 識 is zhì 'to remember, to keep in mind' (Zhu Xi: 識音志，識，記也), though he allows the ordinary reading shí as well. 黙識 is 'not speaking, yet keeping it in the heart'; Zhu Xi records another explanation, 識 = 'to understand' — grasping it in the heart without words — and judges the first nearer the mark. 黙 is the edition's form of 默. 厭 yàn 'to be sated'; 倦 'to weary'. 何有於我哉 'what of it is there in me?' — Zhu Xi: 'which of these do I have?' These three are not even the summit of sagehood, and still he dared not claim them: modesty on modesty. He Yan's Zheng Xuan reads the line the other way: others have none of these practices; I alone have them.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
德之不修，
學之不講，
聞義不能徙，
不善不能改，
是吾憂也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Virtue not cultivated,
learning not gone over,
hearing what is right and not able to move to it,
what is not good and not able to change it —
these are my worries.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “That I may fail to cultivate virtue, fail to go over what I have learned, hear what is right and not move toward it, have faults and not mend them — these are the things that trouble me.”
sentences.n: 德之不修 'virtue's not being cultivated': 之 between subject and verb turns each clause into a noun phrase, and 是 'these' sums up all four as the subject of 吾憂 'my worries'. Virtue and learning stand first as topics; they are what is (not) cultivated, (not) gone over. 講 jiǎng is 'to go over, to discuss and make clear'; 徙 xǐ 'to shift one's place', here toward the right. Zhu Xi quotes Yin Tun: virtue must be cultivated before it is complete, learning discussed before it is clear; seeing the good and moving to it, correcting faults without grudging — these four are the essentials of renewing oneself daily; if the sage still worried over them, how much more should the learner. He Yan's Kong Anguo: the Master constantly worried over these four. Variant: He Yan's text reads 聞義不能從 'not able to follow it' for 徙, and has 也 after each of the first four clauses.

sentences.t:
子之燕居，
申申如也，
夭夭如也。
sentences.l:
The Master at his leisure:
easy and unbent he was,
and cheerful was his look.
sentences.i: When the Master was at home with nothing to attend to, his bearing was relaxed and his face was pleasant.
sentences.n: 子之燕居 'the Master's being at leisure', made a topic by 之. 燕 yàn is 'at ease, at rest' (Zhu Xi: 燕居，閒暇無事之時, times of leisure with no business in hand). 如 after a description means 'the look of, -like'; the doubled words 申申 and 夭夭 are descriptive (cf. 郁郁 3.14). Zhu Xi quotes Yang Shi: 申申 — his bearing was relaxed (舒); 夭夭 — his countenance was glad (愉). And Master Cheng: here the disciples were good at describing the sage; 申申 did not say it all, so they added 夭夭. People at leisure today, if they are not idle and slack, are too stern; neither fits these words — only the sage has of himself the air of balance and ease (中和之氣). He Yan's Ma Rong: the look of mildness and ease (和舒之貌).

sentences.t:
子曰：「
甚矣吾衰也！
久矣吾不復夣見周公。」

morph.gloss: dreamed of (the edition's form of 夢)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Far gone it is, my decline!
Long it is that I have not again dreamed of seeing the Duke of Zhou.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “I have grown very feeble! It has been a long while since the Duke of Zhou came to me in my dreams.”
sentences.n: The predicate stands first for emphasis: 甚矣吾衰也 'extreme — my decline', i.e. 'my decline is far gone'; 久矣… likewise, 'long — that I have not…'. 矣 marks a state now reached. 復 fù 'again' (Zhu Xi: 扶又反). 夣 is the edition's form of 夢 'to dream'. 周公 the Duke of Zhou, brother of King Wu of Zhou, regent for the young King Cheng and credited with the Zhou rites and institutions; Lu was his fief. Zhu Xi: in his prime Confucius meant to carry out the Way of the Duke of Zhou, so in his sleep it was as if he saw him; in old age, unable to carry it out, he no longer had that intent, and no longer the dream — so he sighed at how far he had declined. He quotes Master Cheng: the heart that keeps the Way knows no old or young, but in one who would put the Way into practice, the body grows old and declines. He Yan's Kong Anguo says much the same.

sentences.t:
子曰：
志於道，
sentences.l: The Master said: Set your intent on the Way,
sentences.i: The Master said: Make the Way your aim;
sentences.n: Four clauses of the same build, verb + 於 'on, in' + object, each followed in Zhu Xi's edition by his comment; he reads them as the order a learner should follow. 志 'intent' is where the heart goes (Zhu Xi: 心之所之之謂; cf. 2.4 志于學); 道 is what ought to be done in the daily round of human relations; knowing this and setting the heart on it, one goes straight, without the confusion of byways. He Yan's commentary: 志 is 'to long for' (慕); the Way cannot be embodied, so one sets one's heart on it, that is all.

sentences.t: 據於德，
sentences.l: hold fast to virtue,
sentences.i: keep firm hold of virtue;
sentences.n: 據 jù is 'to grasp and keep' (Zhu Xi: 據音倨，執守之意). 德 virtue, for Zhu Xi, is what one has gained in the heart by walking the Way (行道而有得於心 — he plays on 德 and 得 'to gain'); gained and kept without loss, it is one from beginning to end and renewed day by day. He Yan's commentary: 據 is 'to lean on as on a staff' (杖); virtue has a settled form, so it can be leaned on.

sentences.t: 依於仁，
sentences.l: rely on humaneness,
sentences.i: never depart from humaneness;
sentences.n: 依 is 'not to depart from' (Zhu Xi: 不違之謂). 仁 humaneness is the whole of the heart's virtue once selfish desires are wholly gone; at this stage there is no departing from it even for the space of a meal (cf. 4.5), and everywhere is the flow of Heaven's principle. He Yan's commentary: 依 is 'to lean against' (倚); the work of humaneness reaches others, so it can be leaned on.

sentences.t: 游於藝。
sentences.l: roam at ease in the arts.
sentences.i: and range freely among the arts.
sentences.n: 游 is 'to roam, to take one's pleasure in' (Zhu Xi: 玩物適情之謂). 藝 the arts: the patterns of the rites and music and the methods of archery, charioteering, writing and number (禮樂之文，射御書數之法) — the 'six arts'. Zhu Xi sums up the chapter: in learning nothing comes before setting the intent; set on the Way, the heart rests in what is right; holding to virtue, the Way is gained in the heart and not lost; relying on humaneness, one's virtuous nature is always at work and the pull of things is held off; roaming in the arts, small things are not neglected and both action and rest are nourished. Keep this order of first and last, heavy and light, and root and branch are both covered, inner and outer nourish each other, and one enters the domain of the sages without knowing it. He Yan's commentary: 藝 are the six arts, not things to hold or lean on — hence 'roam'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
自行束脩以上，
吾未嘗無誨焉。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “From those who brought a bundle of dried meat upward,
I have never once been without teaching for them.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Anyone who has come to me with a gift, be it only a bundle of dried meat, has had teaching from me.”
sentences.n: 自…以上 'from … upward' sets a lowest step on a scale: anyone who brings at least this much. 行 xíng 'to carry out', here to present the gift. 脩 xiū is dried meat, and ten strips make a bundle (Zhu Xi: 脩，脯也，十脡為束); in antiquity a first visit had to bring a gift (贄) as the rite, and a bundle of dried meat was the slightest of them. 未嘗無 'never once without' — two negatives make 'always'. 焉 is 'there, for him'. Zhu Xi: all men are born with the same principle, so the sage wished everyone to enter the good; but where people did not come to learn, there is no rite of going to teach them; so whoever came with the rites was always given something. He Yan's Kong Anguo: if a man could offer the rites, from a bundle of dried meat upward, the Master taught him.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
不憤不啓，
不悱不發。
舉一隅不以三隅反，
則不復也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Not straining, I do not open;
not struggling for words, I do not bring out.
I hold up one corner, and if he does not turn back with three corners,
then I do not tell it again.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “I do not open the way for a student until he is straining to understand, nor help him to the words until he is struggling to find them. If I show him one corner of a thing and he cannot work out the other three from it, I do not go over it again.”
sentences.n: Classical Chinese often states a condition with no word for 'if': 不憤不啓 'not straining — (I) do not open'. Zhu Xi: 憤 fèn (房粉反) is the heart seeking to get through and not yet able; 悱 fěi (芳匪反) the look of the mouth wanting to speak and not yet able; 啓 is to open up his thinking, 發 to bring out his words. 啓 is the edition's form of 啟. A thing with four corners: hold up one and the other three can be known; 反 is 'to turn back and check one against the other', 復 fù 'to tell again' (Zhu Xi: 扶又反，再告也). Zhu Xi: the chapter before spoke of the sage's untiring teaching, so this is recorded beside it, to urge learners to make the effort that readies them to be taught. He quotes Master Cheng: straining and struggling are sincere intent showing in the face and words; wait till sincerity is full, then tell; and when told, wait for him to get it himself before telling more; and again: open a man before he strains and struggles, and his knowing will not hold fast; open him after, and it comes in a flood. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: if, shown one corner, a man does not think of the rest of its kind, the Master does not teach him again. Variant: He Yan's text reads 舉一隅而示之 'hold up one corner and show it to him' and 則吾不復 'then I do not (teach) again'.

sentences.t:
子食於有喪者之側，
未嘗飽也。
sentences.l:
The Master, eating at the side of one in mourning,
never once ate his fill.
sentences.i: When the Master ate beside someone in mourning, he never ate his fill.
sentences.n: 有喪者 'one who has a death (to mourn)': 喪 sāng, mourning; 者 makes the phrase 'the one who'. 之側 'at the side of'. Zhu Xi: face to face with mourning one grieves and cannot relish food. He Yan's commentary: to eat one's fill beside a grieving mourner is to lack the feeling of pity.

sentences.t:
子於是日哭，
則不歌。
sentences.l:
On a day the Master had wailed,
he did not sing.
sentences.i: On a day when he had gone to wail with the bereaved, the Master did not sing.
sentences.n: 於是日 'on this day', i.e. on any day when he had wailed. 哭 kū is the formal wailing of mourning; Zhu Xi: 弔哭, wailing on a visit of condolence; within the one day the lingering grief was not forgotten, so he could not, of himself, sing. Zhu Xi prints this line as part of the same chapter, 7.9. He quotes Xie Liangzuo: in these two things the learner can see how right the sage's feelings were; only one who can recognize the sage's feelings and nature can learn the Way. Variant: He Yan's text reads 子於是日也哭, with a pausing 也.

sentences.t:
子謂顏淵曰：「
用之則行，
舍之則藏，
惟我與爾有是夫！」

morph.gloss: Yuan (in 顏淵, from the courtesy name Ziyuan)

sentences.i: The Master said to Yan Yuan: “To go out and act when called on, and to withdraw quietly when passed over — only you and I are capable of that.”
sentences.n: 用之…舍之: 之 is the man who is employed or set aside, and each 則 'then' joins a condition to what follows, with no word for 'if'. 舍 is shě 'to let go, leave unused' (Zhu Xi: 上聲); 行 xíng is to go out and act, 藏 cáng 'to store away', to keep oneself hidden. 夫 fú at the end is an exclamation (Zhu Xi: 音扶). Zhu Xi quotes Yin Tun: whether one is used or set aside has nothing to do with oneself; going forward or withdrawing, one is content with what one meets, and fate is not even worth speaking of; Yanzi was close to a sage, so he too could do it. He Yan's Kong Anguo: when it is right to act, act; when it is right to stop, stop; only I and Yan Yuan are alike in this.

sentences.t:
子路曰：「
子行三軍，
則誰與？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zilu said: “If you, Master, led the three armies,
then whom would you have with you?”
sentences.i: Zilu said: “And if you were in command of the three armies, Master, whom would you take with you?”
sentences.n: 子 here is 'you, Master', in direct address. 誰與 is 與誰 'with whom': a question-word object goes before its verb or preposition. 行 xíng 'to set in motion, to lead'. A 軍 'army' was 12,500 men, and a great state had three (Zhu Xi; Kong Anguo too says a great state had three armies). Zhu Xi: Zilu, seeing the Master praise Yan Yuan alone, and confident in his own courage, supposed that if the Master led the three armies he would surely take Zilu with him.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
暴虎馮河，
死而無悔者，
吾不與也。
必也臨事而懼，
好謀而成者也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “One who fights a tiger bare-handed, wades the River,
and dies with no regret —
him I would not have with me.
It must be one who faces a task with fear,
who loves to plan and brings it off.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A man who would fight a tiger with his bare hands or wade across the River, and die for it without a regret, is not the man I would take. It would have to be someone who goes into an undertaking with due fear, and who likes to lay his plans and see them through.”
sentences.n: 暴 bào is 'to attack bare-handed' and 馮 píng 'to wade' (Zhu Xi: 馮，皮冰反; 暴虎，徒搏；馮河，徒涉 — fighting with no weapon, crossing with no boat; He Yan's Kong Anguo the same); the pair comes from the Ode 'Xiao min' 小旻 (不敢暴虎，不敢馮河). 河 in early texts is the Yellow River. 者 closes the long description: 'one who…'. 吾不與也 answers Zilu's 誰與. 必也…者也 'it must be one who…'. 懼 is, per Zhu Xi, to treat the task with reverence (敬其事); 成 to carry one's plans through (成其謀); 好 hào. Zhu Xi: all of this checks Zilu's courage and teaches him; yet the essentials of leading an army truly lie in nothing else, which Zilu did not know. He quotes Xie Liangzuo: between going forward and withdrawing the sage has no fixed intent and no 'must'; going forward is not coveting office, withdrawing is not keeping one's goodness to oneself; so only Yanzi could share it. Zilu had no greed, but could not be free of fixity, and in asking about the three armies he sank lower; the Master's answer met his fault to save him — without planning nothing succeeds, without fear one is sure to fail; true even of small matters, and how much more of leading the three armies.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
富而可求也，
雖執鞭之士，
吾亦為之。
如不可求，
從吾所好。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “If wealth could be sought,
even as a man who holds the whip
I too would do it.
If it cannot be sought,
I follow what I love.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If wealth were a thing a man could get by seeking, I would go after it even if it meant holding a whip for others. As it is not, I keep to what I love.”
sentences.n: 而 here is 'if' (= 如), as Zhu Xi's paraphrase shows (設言富若可求, 'supposing wealth could be sought'). 執鞭之士 'a man who holds the whip' — Zhu Xi: the work of a lowly man; He Yan's Zheng Xuan: a menial post. 為 wéi 'to do'; 從 cóng; 所好 hào 'what I love'. Zhu Xi: if wealth could be sought, he would not refuse even menial service to get it; but it is fated and not got by seeking, so one rests in what is right — why court disgrace for nothing? He quotes Su Shi: the sage never meant to seek wealth — why ask whether it can be sought? He speaks so only to show that it certainly cannot; and Yang Shi: the gentleman does not hate wealth and rank and refuse to seek them; they lie with Heaven, and there is no way of seeking them. Zheng Xuan puts it otherwise: wealth and rank are not got by seeking, and one should cultivate virtue to get them; but if they could be sought in keeping with the Way, I would take even a menial post. Kong Anguo: what he loves is the way of the ancients. Variant: He Yan's text reads 如不可求者.

sentences.t:
子之所慎：
齊、戰、疾。
sentences.l:
What the Master was careful about:
fasting, war, sickness.
sentences.i: The things the Master treated with particular care were the fast before a sacrifice, war, and illness.
sentences.n: 所 + verb is 'what one …': 所慎 'what he was careful about', and 之 makes 子之所慎 one noun phrase. 齊 is zhāi, the fast and purification before a sacrifice (later written 齋; Zhu Xi: 側皆反). Zhu Xi: 齊 means 'to make even' — before a sacrifice one evens out the unsettled thoughts in order to meet the spirits; whether one's sincerity is complete, and whether the spirits accept the offering, is decided here. In war the life and death of the many and the survival of the state are at stake; in sickness one's own life and death. He quotes Yin Tun: the Master was careful in everything; the disciples recorded the greatest things. He Yan's Kong Anguo: these three are what others cannot be careful about, but the Master could.

sentences.t:
子在齊聞韶，
三月不知肉味。
曰：「不圖為樂之至於斯也！」
sentences.l:
The Master, in Qi, heard the Shao,
and for three months did not know the taste of meat.
He said: “I did not imagine that the making of music could reach this.”
sentences.i: In Qi the Master heard the Shao, and for three months he did not notice the taste of meat. “I never expected,” he said, “that the making of music could come to this.”
sentences.n: 齊 here is qí, the state of Qi. 韶 the Shao is the music of Shun, which 3.25 calls perfectly beautiful and perfectly good. Zhu Xi notes that the Shiji has 學之 before 三月 — he studied it for three months; 不知肉味, his heart was wholly in it and reached nothing else. 不圖 'did not expect'; 為樂 wéi yuè 'the making of music', and 之 turns 為樂至於斯 into the object of 圖. Zhu Xi: he did not expect Shun's making of music to reach such beauty, and sighed deeply. He quotes Fan Zuyu: the Shao was perfect in beauty and in goodness, and music can go no further; so he studied it for three months and admired it so — utmost sincerity, deepest feeling. He Yan's Zhou Shenglie: he heard and practised the splendour of the Shao music, so forgot the taste of meat; Wang Su: 為 is 'to make'; he did not expect Shao music to be made 'here' — 斯 'this' being Qi. Variant: He Yan's text reads 聞韶樂 'heard the Shao music'.

sentences.t:
冉有曰：「
夫子為衞君乎？」
子貢曰：「諾，吾將問之。」

morph.gloss: Ran, a surname (Ran You, Ran Qiu)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Ran You said: “Is the Master for the lord of Wei?”
Zigong said: “Yes — I will ask him.”
sentences.i: Ran You said: “Is the Master on the side of the lord of Wei?” “Very well,” said Zigong, “I shall ask him.”
sentences.n: 夫子 is 'the Master' as the disciples speak of him among themselves. 為 is wèi 'to be for, to help' (Zhu Xi: 去聲，為猶助也; Kong Anguo the same). 衞 is the edition's form of 衛 Wei. The lord of Wei was Duke Chu, Zhe 輒. Zhu Xi tells the story: Duke Ling had driven out his heir Kuaikui 蒯聵; when the duke died the people of Wei set up Kuaikui's son Zhe; then the state of Jin tried to install Kuaikui, and Zhe resisted his own father. Confucius was living in Wei, and the people of Wei held that Kuaikui had offended against his father while Zhe, the heir's son, should rightly rule — hence Ran You's doubt. (Kong Anguo adds that Jin's Zhao Yang put Kuaikui into Qi 戚 and Wei's Shi Manggu besieged him there.) 諾 nuò is a word of assent (應辭); 將 jiāng 'to be about to'.

sentences.t:
入，曰：「伯夷、叔齊何人也？」
曰：「古之賢人也。」
曰：「怨乎？」
曰：「求仁而得仁，又何怨？」
出，曰：「夫子不為也。」

morph.gloss: the Yi, the peoples of the east
to make even, to bring to one standard (Zhu Xi: 所以一之也)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
He went in and said: “Boyi and Shuqi — what men were they?”
He said: “Worthy men of old.”
He said: “Did they regret it?”
He said: “They sought humaneness and got humaneness — what then would they regret?”
He came out and said: “The Master is not for him.”
sentences.i: Zigong went in and asked: “What sort of men were Boyi and Shuqi?” “Worthy men of old.” “Did they regret what they had done?” “They sought humaneness, and humaneness is what they found — what could they regret?” Zigong came out and said: “The Master will not take his side.”
sentences.n: The speakers are not named; Zigong asks, the Master answers. 伯夷 Boyi and 叔齊 Shuqi (5.22), Zhu Xi tells, were the two sons of the lord of Guzhu 孤竹. Their father's dying command was to make Shuqi his heir; when he died Shuqi yielded to Boyi, and Boyi said, 'It was our father's command,' and fled; Shuqi too would not rule, and fled, and the people set up a middle son. Later, when King Wu marched against Zhou 紂 of Shang, the two held his horse's bridle and remonstrated; once Shang had fallen they were ashamed to eat the grain of Zhou, hid on Mount Shouyang and starved. 怨 'to resent' is here, Zhu Xi says, like 悔 'to regret', and we follow him. Because a gentleman living in a state does not find fault with its grandees, still less its ruler, Zigong did not name the lord of Wei but asked about the brothers; the answer made it plain the Master would not help him. Boyi held his father's command highest, Shuqi the bond between brothers; both sought what accorded with Heaven's principle and set the heart at rest, and gave up a state like a worn-out sandal — what was there to regret? Zhe, holding the state and resisting his father, afraid only of losing it, cannot be named in the same breath. He quotes Master Cheng: Boyi and Shuqi yielded the state and fled, remonstrated against the campaign and starved, and never resented or regretted it; the Master held them worthy, so it was clear he would not side with Zhe. He Yan's Kong Anguo: they yielded the state, went far away and died of hunger, so Zigong asked whether they resented it; they took yielding as humaneness — how should they resent it? Zheng Xuan: father and son contending for a state is wicked conduct; the Master held Boyi and Shuqi worthy and humane, so plainly he would not help the lord of Wei. Variant: He Yan's text reads 子曰古之賢人也, naming the speaker, and 又何怨乎.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
飯疏食飲水，
曲肱而枕之，
樂亦在其中矣。
不義而富且貴，
於我如浮雲。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Eating coarse rice, drinking water,
bending an arm and pillowing my head on it —
joy too lies in the midst of these.
Not right, and yet rich and high in rank —
to me that is like floating clouds.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Coarse rice to eat, plain water to drink, the crook of my arm for a pillow — joy is there too, right in the midst of it. Wealth and rank that are not rightly come by are no more to me than clouds drifting by.”
sentences.n: 飯 fàn is a verb here, 'to eat' (Zhu Xi: 飯，食之也; 符晚反). 疏食 shū sì is 'coarse grain, coarse rice' (Zhu Xi: 麤飯; 食音嗣, cf. 6.9 簞食). 曲肱 'to bend the forearm'; 枕 'to pillow one's head on' — Zhu Xi marks the verb 去聲 zhèn; modern practice reads zhěn, which we give. 樂 lè 'joy' (Zhu Xi: 音洛). 不義而富且貴: 而 'and yet', 且 'and also'. Zhu Xi: the sage's heart is wholly Heaven's principle, so even in the extremity of hardship joy is everywhere present; he looks on wealth and rank that are not right as on floating clouds that are not there at all — nothing in him is moved. He quotes Master Cheng: it is not that he enjoyed coarse food and water, but that even coarse food and water could not change his joy; and again: you must know what it is that is enjoyed. Variant: He Yan's text writes 疏 with the grass radical (𬞞, i.e. 蔬 'vegetables'), and his Kong Anguo glosses 蔬食 as 'vegetable food' (菜食) — 'eating vegetables' rather than 'coarse rice'; he glosses 肱 as 'arm'. Zheng Xuan: wealth and rank not got by what is right are to me like floating clouds — not my own.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
加我數年，
五十以學易，
可以無大過矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Add to me several years,
at fifty to study the Changes,
and I could be without great faults.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If my years were lengthened a little, so that at fifty I could study the Changes, I might avoid any great fault.”
sentences.n: 加 'to add (to)'; 數 shù 'several'; 易 yì is the Changes, the Book of Changes 易經; 以 'so as to', 可以 'can thereby'. The printed line is hard, and Zhu Xi doubts it. He records that Liu Mianzhi heard Liu Anshi say he had read another text of the Analects with 假 'to grant' for 加 and 卒 'to the end' for 五十 — 加 and 假 confused because they sound alike, 卒 wrongly split into 五 and 十; and he adds that the Shiji has 假我數年，若是，我於易則彬彬矣 'grant me some years, and in the Changes I would be accomplished' — 假 for 加, and no 五十; Confucius was then nearly seventy, so 五十 is surely an error. On that text the line is 'grant me some years to finish studying the Changes'. Zhu Xi: study of the Changes makes clear the principles of good and ill fortune, waxing and waning, advance and retreat, survival and ruin, so one can be without great faults; the sage saw that the Way of the Changes is endless and said this to teach that it must be studied and must not be studied lightly. He Yan's commentary takes 五十 as an age: the Changes exhaust principle and fulfil nature to reach the decree (命); at fifty one knows the decree of Heaven (2.4), and at that age one reads the book that reaches to the decree. Variant: one collation witness (Ruan's reprint) reads 亦 for 易 — 五十以學，亦可以無大過矣 'at fifty to study, and I too could be without great faults', with no Changes at all; this is the reading Lu Deming records for the old Lu text of the Analects (魯讀易為亦).

sentences.t:
子所雅言：
詩、書、執禮，
皆雅言也。
sentences.l:
What the Master constantly spoke of:
the Odes, the Documents, keeping the rites —
all these he constantly spoke of.
sentences.i: What the Master talked of again and again was the Odes, the Documents and the keeping of the rites: these were his constant themes.
sentences.n: Zhu Xi: 雅 is 'constant, regular' (常也) and 執 'to keep' (守也). The Odes order the feelings and one's nature, the Documents speak of government, the rites keep one careful of measure and form (節文) — all bear on the realities of the daily round, so he spoke of them constantly; of the rites alone it says 'keep', because they are what a man holds to in practice, not merely recites and expounds. He quotes Master Cheng: this is as far as Confucius's ordinary talk went; human nature and the Way of Heaven could not be heard of (5.12) — the point is to know them silently (7.2); and Xie Liangzuo: this was recorded beside the saying on studying the Changes as of a kind. He Yan's commentary reads 雅言 differently: Kong Anguo takes it as 'correct speech' (正言), and Zheng Xuan says that in reading the canons of the former kings the Master always gave their sounds correctly, so that the meaning came through whole; the rites are not recited, hence 'keep'. On that reading, these were the texts the Master recited in the standard pronunciation.

sentences.t:
葉公問孔子於子路，
子路不對。

sentences.l:
The Duke of Ye asked Zilu about Kongzi;
Zilu did not answer.
sentences.i: The Duke of Ye asked Zilu what sort of man Kongzi was, and Zilu gave him no answer.
sentences.n: 葉公 the Duke of Ye was Shen Zhuliang 沈諸梁, courtesy name Zigao 子高, governor (尹) of the county of Ye in Chu; 'duke' was a title he had no right to (Zhu Xi: 僭稱公; He Yan's Kong Anguo says the same). Zhu Xi reads 葉 shè (舒涉反), the old reading of the place name; standard Mandarin now reads it yè, which we give. 問 X 於 Y is 'to ask Y about X'. 子路 Zilu is Zhong You 仲由 (2.17). Why no answer? Zhu Xi offers two guesses: the Duke did not know Confucius, so he must have asked something he had no business asking; or else a sage's virtue is truly hard to put a name to. Kong Anguo: Zilu did not know how to answer.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
女奚不曰：
其為人也，
發憤忘食，
樂以忘憂，
不知老之將至云爾。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “Why didn't you say that he is a man who, once roused to the effort, forgets to eat; who takes such delight in it that his cares slip from his mind; who has not noticed old age creeping up on him — that, and nothing more?”
sentences.n: 女 is rǔ, 'you', the word later written 汝. 奚 'why'. 其為人也 'as for his being a man' (為 wéi): 其 + verb phrase + 也 makes a topic, and what follows says what he is. 發憤 is 'to rouse oneself to effort'; 樂 is lè, 'to take joy'; 將 jiāng 'about to'. 不知老之將至: 之 between subject and verb turns 'old age is about to come' into the object of 知. 云爾 closes a report, 'so it is, just that', adding nothing more. Zhu Xi: when he has not yet got a thing he is roused and forgets to eat; once he has it he delights in it and forgets his cares; between the two he bends to it day after day and does not notice his years running short. He only speaks, Zhu Xi says, of how earnest his love of learning is; but savour it and you see a sage's unceasing purity, beyond anyone else's reach. Variant: He Yan's text reads 老之將至也云爾, adding only a particle.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
我非生而知之者，
好古，
敏以求之者也。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “I was not born knowing anything. I love the ancients, and I have gone after what they knew with all the speed I could.”
sentences.n: 生而知之者 'one who is born and knows it' — knowledge without study; 者 makes the whole phrase 'one who…', and 非…者也 'is not one who…'. 好 is hào, 'to love' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). Zhu Xi glosses 敏 as 速 'quick', meaning 汲汲 'pressing eagerly after'. One born knowing, he says, has a clear, bright endowment and sees what is right without needing to learn. He quotes Yin Tun: Confucius, a sage who knew from birth, always called himself fond of learning, and not only to spur others on; what can be known at birth is moral principle, but the rites and music, the names of things, and the changes of past and present must still be learned before one can check them against the facts. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: he says this to encourage men to learn. Variant: He Yan's text reads 敏而求之 'quick, and seeking it'.

sentences.t: 子不語怪，力，亂，神。
sentences.l: The Master did not talk of the uncanny, of strength, of disorder, of spirits.
sentences.i: Strange happenings, deeds of sheer might, rebellion, and the doings of gods and ghosts — these the Master would not discuss.
sentences.n: 語 yǔ here is 'to talk about, discuss'. Four single nouns stand as objects of one verb. Zhu Xi: 怪 is the strange and freakish, 力 feats of courage and strength, 亂 rebellion and disorder — none of them the right course of things, so the sage did not speak of them; spirits (鬼神), the traces of creation, are not wrong, but they are hard to make clear unless one has gone to the bottom of principle, so he did not talk of them lightly either. He quotes Xie Liangzuo: the sage spoke of the constant, not the strange; of virtue, not force; of order, not disorder; of men, not spirits. He Yan's Kong Anguo gives examples: strength like Ao's, who pushed a boat over dry land, or Wu Huo's, who lifted a thousand jun; disorder like a minister killing his lord or a son his father; spirits, the business of ghosts and gods — things either of no use to teaching, or which he could not bear to speak of.

sentences.t:
子曰：「三人行，
必有我師焉。
擇其善者而從之，
其不善者而改之。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Three men walking —
there is sure to be my teacher among them.
I pick out what is good in them and follow it;
what is not good in them, I correct.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Put me on the road with any two others and I will find a teacher there. What is good in them I take up and follow; what is not good I look for in myself and mend.”
sentences.n: 行 xíng 'to walk, travel'. 焉 'in it, among them' (the fused 於之). 其善者 'their good ones' — 者 turns 'their good' into 'what is good in them'; the second 其不善者 is fronted as topic of 改之. Zhu Xi: of three walking together, one is myself; of the other two, one is good and one bad; I follow the good and correct in myself the bad, so both are my teachers. He quotes Yin Tun, citing 4.17: 'seeing worth, think of being level with it; seeing the unworthy, search within yourself' — then good and bad are both my teachers, and how can advance in goodness ever run out? He Yan's commentary: among three there is no fixed worth or folly; he chooses the good and corrects the bad, and so has no fixed teacher. Variant: He Yan's text reads 我三人行，必得我師焉 'when I walk with two others I am sure to get my teacher'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「天生德於予，
桓魋其如予何？」

morph.gloss: Huan Tui — Xiang Tui, minister of war in Song

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Heaven brought forth virtue in me;
what then can Huan Tui do about me?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “It was Heaven that bred virtue in me. How could Huan Tui touch me?”
sentences.n: 予 yú 'I, me'. 如 X 何 is a fixed frame, 'what (can one) do with X?'; here 如予何 'what can he do to me?', and 其 adds 'then, after all'. 桓魋 Huan Tui (魋 tuí, Zhu Xi: 徒雷反) was Xiang Tui 向魋, minister of war (司馬) in Song; descended from Duke Huan of Song, he was also called by the clan name Huan. Zhu Xi says only that Tui wanted to harm Confucius, and reads the line: since Heaven has endowed me with such virtue, Huan Tui can do nothing to me — he cannot go against Heaven to harm me. He Yan's Bao Xian: Heaven gave him a sage's nature; his virtue matches Heaven and Earth, all is auspicious and nothing goes against him — hence 'what can he do to me?'

sentences.t:
子曰：「
二三子以我為隱乎？
吾無隱乎爾。
吾無行而不與二三子者，
是丘也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “My friends, do you take me for one who hides things?
I hide nothing from you.
There is nothing I do that I do not show you, my friends —
that is Qiu.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “My friends, do you suppose I hide things from you? I hide nothing. Whatever I do, I do in front of you, my friends — that is simply how Qiu is.”
sentences.n: 二三子 'you two or three', the Master to his disciples (3.24). 以 A 為 B 'to take A as B' (為 wéi). 乎 in 吾無隱乎爾 is the preposition 'from', = 於. 無 X 而不 Y 者 'there is no X that is not Y': 'nothing I do that I do not show'. 與 is yǔ, which Zhu Xi glosses 示 'to show'; He Yan's Bao Xian takes it as 'to share': 'there is nothing I do that I do not do with you'. 丘 is Confucius naming himself. Zhu Xi: the disciples found the Master's Way so high and deep they could not come near it, and suspected him of keeping something back, not knowing that in a sage action and rest, speech and silence are all teaching. He quotes Master Cheng: the sage's Way is like Heaven; if the disciples truly thought it out of reach, their will to go towards it would slacken, so the sage always stoops to meet them; and Lü Dalin: the sage embodies the Way and hides nothing — like the bright signs of Heaven, all is plain teaching, and it is men who fail to look. Variants: He Yan's text reads 以我為隱子乎 'do you take me as hiding things, sirs?' and 吾無所行而不與 with 所, the same sense.

sentences.t:
子以四敎：
文，行，忠，信。
sentences.l:
The Master taught by four things:
letters, conduct, wholeheartedness, good faith.
sentences.i: There were four things the Master taught: letters, conduct, wholeheartedness, and keeping good faith.
sentences.n: 以 X 敎 'to teach by means of X'; the four follow as a list. 敎 is the edition's form of 教 jiào. Zhu Xi reads 行 xìng, 'conduct' (去聲), a tone distinction modern practice does not keep; we give xíng. He quotes Master Cheng: the Master taught men to study letters and cultivate their conduct and to hold on to being wholehearted and true to their word — and 忠 and 信 are the root. He Yan's commentary: these four have form and substance and can be taken up and taught.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
聖人，吾不得而見之矣；
得見君子者，斯可矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “A sage — I do not get to see one;
to get to see a gentleman — that would do.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A sage I shall never get to see. To see a gentleman would be enough.”
sentences.n: 聖人 'the sage' and 君子 'the gentleman' are two grades. Zhu Xi: 聖人 is the name for one whose spirit and clarity are past fathoming; 君子 the name for one whose talent and virtue stand out from the crowd. 不得而見之 'I do not get to see him'; 得見…者 'getting to see…' is a topic, picked up by 斯 'that, then' and judged 可 'would do', as in 5.19 再，斯可矣. He Yan's commentary reads the saying politically: the Master is grieving that the age has no enlightened ruler.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
善人，吾不得而見之矣；
得見有恒者，斯可矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “A good man — I do not get to see one;
to get to see one who has constancy — that would do.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A truly good man I shall never get to see. If I could see a man who simply held steady, that would be enough.”
sentences.n: The same frame as the line before, one grade lower: 善人 the good man and 有恒者 'one who has constancy' (恒 héng, the edition's form of 恆; Zhu Xi: 胡登反). Zhu Xi thinks the words 子曰 here are an intrusion, since the passage runs on as one saying. 恒 is the sense of 'constant and lasting'. He quotes Zhang Zai: one who has constancy does not divide his heart; the good man has set his heart on humaneness and has no evil.

sentences.t:
亡而為有，
虚而為盈，
約而為泰，
難乎有恒矣。
sentences.i: People who have nothing and act as if they had plenty, who are empty and act as if they were full, who are pinched and act as if they lived at ease — it is hard for such people to keep steady.
sentences.n: 亡 is read wú here, the same word as 無 'not to have' (Zhu Xi: 亡讀為無). Three lines of one shape, A 而 為 B: 'being A, yet playing at B' — 為 wéi 'to make, to act as'. 約 'pinched, straitened' against 泰 'ample, lavish'. 難乎…矣 'hard indeed…'; 乎 here only adds weight. Zhu Xi: all three are empty show, and whoever is like this cannot keep to the constant. He quotes Zhang Shi: 'sage' and 'gentleman' speak of learning, 'good man' and 'one with constancy' of native quality; and adds his own comment: the distance between the man of constancy and the sage is vast, yet no one has reached sagehood without starting from constancy — which is why the passage ends by dwelling on it, showing the gate into virtue. He Yan's Kong Anguo: such men are hard to call constant.

sentences.t:
子釣而不綱，
弋不射宿。
sentences.l:
The Master fished by hook and line, not by rope-net;
he shot with the corded arrow, but not at birds at roost.
sentences.i: The Master would fish with a rod and line, but never stretch a net across the stream; he would bring down birds with a corded arrow, but never one asleep on its perch.
sentences.n: 釣 'to fish with hook and line'. 綱, as Zhu Xi describes it, is fishing with a net hung on a great rope stretched right across the stream (He Yan's Kong Anguo: a great rope across the current with many lines hung from it) — taking everything that swims. 弋 yì is shooting with an arrow tied to a cord of raw silk, so bird and arrow can be drawn back; 宿 sù is a bird roosting for the night. Zhu Xi gives 射 an old reading (食亦反) that modern practice does not keep; we give shè. Both nouns 綱 and 弋 are used here as verbs. Zhu Xi quotes Hong Xingzu: Confucius was poor and lowly when young and sometimes had to fish and shoot to feed his parents and supply the sacrifices; but to take every creature, or catch one off guard, he would not do — here you see a humane man's heart: as he treats creatures, so he treats men; as in small things, so in great.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
蓋有不知而作之者，
我無是也。
多聞，擇其善者而從之；
多見而識之：
知之次也。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “There may be those who make things without knowing —
I have none of this.
Hearing much, I pick out the good in it and follow it;
seeing much, I remember it:
this is next to knowing.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “There are perhaps people who go and make things up without understanding them. That is not my way. I hear a great deal and choose the good in it to follow; I see a great deal and keep it in mind. That is the next best thing to knowing.”
sentences.n: 蓋 opens a guess, 'there may be'. 作 is 'to make, to originate'; Zhu Xi: 不知而作 is to act or make without knowing the principle — reckless making; Confucius says he has never done it, which is modest, but shows too that there was nothing he did not know. He Yan's Bao Xian: many men of the time forced the sense and made up writings recklessly. 識 is read zhì, 'to remember' (Zhu Xi: 識音志，記也). 多聞，多見 echo 2.18. Zhu Xi: what one follows must be chosen, but what one records keeps the good and the bad alike, for comparison; such a man, though he has not yet truly grasped the principle, ranks next to one who knows. 知之次 'the next after knowing it'. Variant: He Yan's text reads 知次也 without the second 之; Kong Anguo: such a one comes next to those who know.

sentences.t:
互鄉難與言，
童子見，
門人惑。
sentences.i: The people of Huxiang were not easy to reason with. When a boy from there was received by the Master, the disciples did not know what to make of it.
sentences.n: 互鄉 Huxiang is the name of a district. 難與言 'hard to talk with': Zhu Xi says its people were steeped in bad ways and hard to speak to of the good; He Yan's Zheng Xuan, that they spoke wilfully and did not fit the times. 童子 a boy, not yet capped. 見 is read xiàn, 'to be presented, to be received' (Zhu Xi: 賢遍反). 惑 'perplexed': Zhu Xi, the disciples doubted that the Master ought to have seen him.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
與其進也，
不與其退也，
唯何甚？
人潔己以進，
與其潔也，
不保其往也。」

morph.gloss: only — (Zhu Xi suspects words lost here)

sentences.i: The Master said: “I approve of his coming to me; that is not approving of whatever he may do once he has gone away. Why be so harsh? When a man has made himself clean to come forward, accept the cleanness he brings; you cannot answer for what he did before.”
sentences.n: The print has 已, a misprint for 己, corrected here. (人潔己 'a man purifies himself' needs 己 'oneself'; our first collation witness reads 絜己, and the Siku copy confuses 己, 已 and 巳 throughout, as at 4.14.) 與 here is yǔ, 'to grant, approve' (Zhu Xi: 與許也) — not the 與其…寧 'rather than…' of 3.4 and 7.35. 潔 'to clean, put in order' (Zhu Xi: 脩治也); 保 'to guarantee, answer for'; 往 'the past, former days' (Zhu Xi: 前日也). Zhu Xi suspects the bamboo slips are out of order: the fourteen characters 人潔…往也 belong before 與其進也, and words may be missing around 唯. Read so: when a man cleans himself and comes, accept only that he has cleaned himself — you cannot answer for the good or ill of his past; approve only his coming to see me, not anything bad he does after he withdraws. Do not chase his past or anticipate his future; when he comes with this heart, simply receive him. He quotes Master Cheng: so broad was the sage in dealing with others. He Yan's Kong Anguo takes 唯何甚 as the Master's rebuke: 'you blame me for seeing this boy — why hate the bad so severely?'; and his Zheng Xuan reads 往 as 'going away': one cannot guarantee how he will act after he leaves.

sentences.t:
子曰：「仁遠乎哉？
我欲仁，
斯仁至矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Is humaneness far away?
I want humaneness,
and here humaneness has come.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Is humaneness so remote? Let me want it, and there it is.”
sentences.n: 乎哉 doubles the question particles: 'is it far — how could it be?', a rhetorical question expecting no. 遠 yuǎn 'far'. 斯 'then, at once' links the wanting to the arriving, and 矣 marks the new state: it has come. Zhu Xi: humaneness is the virtue of the heart, not something outside; let the heart wander off without seeking it and it seems far, but turn back and seek it and it is right here. He quotes Master Cheng: being humane comes from oneself (為仁由己); want it and it comes — what distance is there? He Yan's Bao Xian: the way of humaneness is not far; to practise it is to have arrived.

sentences.t:
陳司敗問：「昭公知禮乎？」
孔子曰：「知禮。」

morph.gloss: the Minister of Crime of Chen
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Minister of Crime of Chen asked: “Did Duke Zhao know the rites?”
Kongzi said: “He knew the rites.”
sentences.i: The Minister of Crime of Chen asked whether Duke Zhao had known the rites. Kongzi said: “He did.”
sentences.n: 陳 Chen is the state; 司敗 is an office, the same as 司寇 'Minister of Crime' elsewhere (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Kong Anguo: a grandee of Chen). 昭公 Duke Zhao of Lu, personal name Chou 稠, was practised in the forms of ceremonial deportment and was thought in his day to know the rites, Zhu Xi says — so the minister asked, and Confucius answered so. Duke Zhao was his own former lord, and Lu his home state. Variant: He Yan's text reads 孔子對曰, the formal 'answered' used to a superior.

sentences.t:
孔子退，
揖巫馬期而進之，曰：「
吾聞君子不黨，
君子亦黨乎？
君取於吳，為同姓，
謂之吳孟子。
君而知禮，
孰不知禮？」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Kongzi withdrew;
the minister bowed Wuma Qi forward and said: “I have heard that the gentleman does not side with his own —
does the gentleman too take sides?
Your lord took a wife from Wu, of the same surname,
and called her Wu Mengzi.
If your lord knew the rites,
who does not know the rites?”
sentences.i: When Kongzi had gone, the minister bowed to Wuma Qi, drew him aside and said: “I had heard that a gentleman does not cover for his own. Does a gentleman take sides after all? Your lord married a woman of Wu, who bore the same surname as he, and to hide it called her Wu Mengzi. If your lord knew the rites, who is there that doesn't?”
sentences.n: 巫馬期 Wuma Qi — surname Wuma, courtesy name Qi, personal name Shi 施 — was a disciple (Zhu Xi; Kong Anguo). It is the minister who bows to him and draws him forward (Zhu Xi: 司敗揖而進之). 黨 dǎng: 'to help one another hide wrongs is called 黨' (Zhu Xi and Kong Anguo alike: 相助匿非曰黨). 取 is read qǔ and means 'to take a wife', the word later written 娶. The rites forbid marrying someone of one's own surname, and Lu and Wu were both of the Ji 姬 clan; a wife from Wu should have been styled Wu Ji 吳姬 (Kong Anguo). Calling her 吳孟子 'Wu Mengzi' hid this, Zhu Xi says, as though she were the eldest (孟) daughter of the Zi 子 surname of Song. (Not Mencius.) 君而知禮，孰不知禮 is the same frame as 3.22: 而 between subject and verb marks a supposition, 'if your lord knew…'. Variants: He Yan's text lacks 君子亦黨乎 altogether, so the minister goes straight from 'the gentleman does not take sides' to the marriage; it also writes 娶 for 取.

sentences.t:
巫馬期以告。
子曰：「丘也幸，
苟有過，
人必知之。」

morph.gloss: a shaman, a medium for spirits
Qi, the courtesy name of Wuma Shi in 巫馬期

sentences.l:
Wuma Qi reported it.
The Master said: “I, Qiu, am fortunate:
if I have a fault,
others are sure to know of it.”
sentences.i: Wuma Qi passed this on. The Master said: “How lucky I am! Whenever I err, there is always someone to know it.”
sentences.n: 以告 'reported (it)', the object of 以 understood. 丘也幸 'as for Qiu, fortunate': the Master names himself. 苟 'if, if ever'. Zhu Xi: Confucius could not say that he had been covering his lord's wrong, nor could he call marrying one of the same surname knowing the rites; so he took it upon himself as his fault and offered no excuse. He quotes Wu Yu: Lu was the Master's parents' state and Duke Zhao a former lord; the minister had not named the matter but suddenly asked whether the duke knew the rites, so the answer was right as given; when the minister called it taking sides, the Master accepted it as a fault, yet still did not say what the fault was, as if he did not know about Mengzi — a pattern for ten thousand generations. He Yan's Kong Anguo: to conceal the wrongs of one's state is itself the rites; the sage, wise and broad, accepted it as a fault.

sentences.t:
子與人歌而善，
必使反之，
而後和之。
sentences.l:
When the Master sang with others and one sang well,
he would always have him repeat it,
and only then join in.
sentences.i: When the Master was singing in company and someone sang a song well, he would always have the singer go through it once more, and only then take up the song with him.
sentences.n: 與 yǔ 'with'. 反 'to go back over, repeat' (Zhu Xi: 反復也). 而後 'and only after that'. 和 is read hè, 'to sing in answer, join in' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). Zhu Xi: he had the singer repeat it because he wanted to catch it in detail and take in what was good in it; he joined in afterwards because he was glad to have caught it and wished to show approval. In one small act, he says, you see the sage's ease and sincerity, his modesty and care, and his unwillingness to cover over another's merit. He Yan's commentary: he delighted in its goodness, so he had it sung again and then joined in himself.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
文，莫吾猶人也；
躬行君子，
則吾未之有得。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: The Master said: “In learning and letters I may be about as good as the next man. But to live as a gentleman in everything I do — that I have not yet managed.”
sentences.n: Zhu Xi takes 莫 as a word of doubt, 'perhaps': 'in letters, perhaps I am like others' — not beyond them, but able to keep up. 躬 'in one's own person'; 行 xíng 'to practise'. 未之有得 'not yet have attained it': after a negative, the pronoun object 之 comes before the verb (as 1.16 不己知). Zhu Xi: both halves are modesty, but they show how much harder, and more urgent, doing is than saying, and he wants men to work at the real thing. He quotes Xie Liangzuo: in letters even the sage is no different from others, so he did not demur; but living out the gentleman is the way into sagehood, so he did not claim it. He Yan's commentary reads the line differently: 莫 is 無 'not', and 文莫 is like the colloquial 文不 — 'in letters, am I not like others?', that is, in all letters I do not surpass others. Variant: He Yan's text ends 未之有得也; Kong Anguo: to be a gentleman in his own person, he had not yet attained it.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
若聖與仁，則吾豈敢？
抑為之不厭，
誨人不倦，
則可謂云爾已矣。」
公西華曰：「正唯弟子不能學也。」

morph.gloss: deference to elders, a younger brother's duty (later written 悌)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “As for sageness and humaneness — how would I dare?
But to do it and never tire,
to teach others and never weary of it —
that much can be said, and no more.”
Gongxi Hua said: “Precisely this is what we disciples cannot learn.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Sage? Humane? How could I presume to claim either? Only that I work at it and never tire, and that I teach others and never weary of it — that much may be said of me, and nothing more.” Gongxi Hua said: “And that is just what we disciples cannot learn to do.”
sentences.n: 若 'as for'; 豈敢 'how would I dare?' (豈 qǐ, a rhetorical 'how'), with the claim left unsaid. 抑 'but, only', turning to what he will admit. 為之 'doing it' (為 wéi): Zhu Xi, practising the Way of humaneness and sageness, and 誨人 teaching others the same. 不厭…不倦 'never tiring…never wearying' — 誨人不倦 is the phrase of 7.2. 可謂云爾已矣 'it can be said so, and that is all' — Zhu Xi: a phrase meaning 'nothing else' (無他之辭). Zhu Xi: sageness is greatness that transforms, humaneness the whole virtue of the heart and the full human Way; but never to tire and never to weary is impossible unless one has them oneself — so the disciples cannot learn it. Chao Yuezhi, quoted by Zhu Xi: men of the time were calling the Master sage and humane, so he declined the names; yet had he only declined, there would be nothing to draw on the world's talents, and sageness and humaneness would become empty vessels no one could reach — so he still placed himself as one who works at them unwearied. Gongxi Hua, Zhu Xi adds, sighed in admiration and knew the Master's meaning deeply. 公西華 Gongxi Hua is Gongxi Chi 公西赤, courtesy name Zihua (5.7, 6.3); 正唯 'exactly this'. He Yan's Bao Xian: 'just as you say: we disciples cannot learn even this, let alone humaneness and sageness.'

sentences.t:
子疾病，
子路請禱。
子曰：「有諸？」
子路對曰：「
有之。
誄曰：『禱爾于上下神祗。』」
子曰：「丘之禱久矣。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
above and below — Heaven and Earth
the spirits of heaven and earth
spirits of earth (祗 for 祇 qí)

sentences.l:
The Master was gravely ill; Zilu asked leave to pray.
The Master said: “Is there such a thing?”
Zilu answered: “There is.
The Lei says: ‘Prayer is made for you to the spirits of Heaven and Earth, above and below.’”
The Master said: “Qiu's praying has gone on a long time.”
sentences.i: When the Master was very ill, Zilu asked to offer prayers for him. The Master said: “Is that done?” Zilu answered: “It is. The Lei says: ‘For you we call on the gods of Heaven above and the spirits of Earth below.’” The Master said: “My own praying began long ago.”
sentences.n: 疾病 'ill, and the illness grave': 病 is the worse stage of 疾. 請 'to ask leave'. 諸 here is the fused 之乎 'it?': 有諸 'is there this?' Zhu Xi: the Master asks whether there is any such principle; He Yan's Zhou Shenglie: whether there is such a practice as praying to the spirits for someone. 誄 lěi (Zhu Xi: 力軌反) is, Zhu Xi says, a eulogy mourning the dead and recounting his deeds; He Yan's Kong Anguo, the title of a collection of prayers. 爾 'you'; 于 = 於 'to'. 上下 Heaven and Earth (Zhu Xi: 上下謂天地): the spirits of Heaven are 神, those of Earth 祇 qí — the edition writes 祗 for 祇, in the text and in Zhu Xi's comment (地曰祗). Zhu Xi: prayer is repenting faults and turning to the good to ask the spirits' help; the sage had no faults to repent and his conduct had long accorded with the spirits — hence 'my praying has gone on long'. He adds that the rites for a dying officer prescribe prayers to the five household spirits, an urgent feeling of servants and sons that need not first be put to the sick man; so Confucius did not refuse Zilu outright, only told him there was no need. Kong Anguo: Zilu missed the point. Variant: He Yan's text reads 丘之禱之久矣.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
奢則不孫，
儉則固。
與其不孫也，
寧固。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Lavish, and so not modest;
sparing, and so shabby.
Rather than immodest,
better shabby.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A lavish man forgets his place; a sparing one grows shabby. Better shabby than forgetting one's place.”
sentences.n: 孫 is read xùn here, the word later written 遜 'compliant, modest' (Zhu Xi: 去聲，順也) — not sūn 'grandson'. 固 'mean, shabby' (Zhu Xi: 陋也). 則 'then' joins condition and result. 與其 A 也，寧 B 'rather than A, better B' is the frame of 3.4 (禮，與其奢也，寧儉). Zhu Xi: both lavishness and thrift miss the mean, but lavishness does the greater harm. He quotes Chao Yuezhi: it is said because it had to be, to correct the faults of the age. He Yan's Kong Anguo: both are failings, but lavishness is worse than thrift — the lavish man oversteps his superiors, the thrifty one only falls short of the rites.

sentences.t:
子曰：「君子坦蕩蕩，
小人長戚戚。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman is level, broad and open;
the small man is forever anxious and distressed.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The gentleman's heart lies open and level, with room to spare; the small man is never free of worry.”
sentences.n: Two lines of one shape: subject, then a description ending in a doubled word. 坦 'level, smooth' (Zhu Xi: 平也); 蕩蕩 'broad and wide' (寬廣貌) — doubling an adjective makes it describe a look or manner. 長 is cháng, 'long, always'; 戚戚 'anxious and distressed'. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: the gentleman follows principle, so he is always unhurried and at peace; the small man is driven by things, so he has many worries — and again, citing the Great Learning: 'the heart broad, the body at ease'. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: 坦蕩蕩 is a look of breadth, 長戚戚 a look of much worry and fear.

sentences.t:
子温而厲，
威而不猛，
恭而安。
sentences.l:
The Master was gentle and yet grave,
imposing and yet not fierce,
courteous and yet at peace.
sentences.i: The Master was warm but firm; he carried authority without menace; he was courteous and yet entirely at his ease.
sentences.n: Three pairs joined by 而 'and yet', each quality held in check by its opposite. 温 is the edition's form of 溫 'gentle' (1.10 夫子溫良恭儉讓); 厲 'grave, stern' (Zhu Xi: 嚴肅也); 威 'imposing, commanding awe'; 猛 'fierce'. Zhu Xi: every man's nature is complete, but the endowment of qi he receives is seldom without a bias; only in the sage was the whole of it perfectly blended, yin and yang matched in virtue, so that this balanced spirit showed in his face and bearing. The disciples watched closely and recorded it in detail — and only one wise enough to know a sage and skilled in describing virtue could have done so; which is why, Zhu Xi says, Master Cheng took these to be Master Zeng's words. The passage closes Book 7.
